questions.title: Origin of the notochord
questions.question: The notochord is derived from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Endoderm is what the invaginating epiblast cells become as they replace the hypoblast during gastrulation -- the notochord forms from a separate, more medial stream of epiblast cells and is not itself endoderm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hypoblast is displaced rather than converted during gastrulation -- it does not contribute cells to the notochord (or to any of the trilaminar disc's three layers, all of which trace back to the epiblast alone).
explanations.C: Incorrect as the direct source, though the notochord is often loosely grouped with mesoderm functionally -- in this bank's own teaching framework the notochord is one of the structures the invaginating epiblast forms directly, alongside the endoderm and the intraembryonic mesoderm, rather than a further derivative of the mesoderm layer itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ectoderm is what remains of the epiblast once the invaginating cells have left to form the other layers -- the notochord forms from cells that migrate cranially through the primitive node before that remainder becomes 'ectoderm' as a named layer.
explanations.E: Correct. Gastrulation begins with epiblast cells proliferating and invaginating through the primitive streak and node. Cells migrating cranially in the midline from the primitive pit form the prenotochordal process, which becomes the notochordal plate and then folds into the definitive notochord. Every layer and axial structure formed during gastrulation -- endoderm, intraembryonic mesoderm, ectoderm and the notochord alike -- traces back to the epiblast as its single source.

questions.learning_objective: State that the notochord, like every layer formed during gastrulation, traces back to the epiblast.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.17, row 45 = e, remark 'Notochord is derived from roof of yolk sac' (page 19 prose) and 'Notoc[hord]' (p.18 letter table) -- both point to option e (epiblast) as printed

questions.title: Neurenteric canal connection
questions.question: Amniotic cavity is temporarily connected to the yolk sac cavity via:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The oral (oropharyngeal) membrane is where ectoderm and endoderm fuse at the cranial end of the embryonic disc -- its breakdown later opens the mouth into the foregut, not a connection between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The allantois is an outpouching of the hindgut into the connecting stalk, involved in early waste handling and later contributing to bladder development -- it is not the structure that links the amniotic cavity to the yolk sac.
explanations.C: Correct. During notochord formation, the roof of the notochordal canal lies against ectoderm and its floor is fused with endoderm; when that floor degenerates, it opens the neurenteric canal, a temporary communication running through the region of the primitive node that connects the amniotic cavity above with the yolk sac cavity below. It closes again once the notochordal plate folds into the definitive notochord and the endoderm re-fuses beneath it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vitello-intestinal (vitelline) duct connects the secondary yolk sac to the midgut later in development, once the gut tube has formed by folding -- a different structure from the neurenteric canal, which exists earlier and connects the amniotic cavity to the yolk sac, not the yolk sac to the gut.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The cloacal membrane is where ectoderm and endoderm fuse at the caudal end of the embryonic disc -- its later breakdown opens the anorectal canal and urogenital sinus to the surface, not a connection between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac.

questions.learning_objective: State that the neurenteric canal is the temporary communication between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac, formed during notochord development.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.19, row 50 = c, remark 'Neurenteric canal forms a temporary connection between amniotic cavity & yolk sac'
field_notes.asu: Embryo 3 Q50, same fact re-tested at Q70 (held as duplicate).

questions.title: The notochord's fate
questions.question: The notochord:

options.A: Is derived from the roof of the yolk sac
options.B: Forms the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc
options.C: Is found caudal to the cloacal membrane
options.E: Forms the bodies of the vertebrae

explanations.A: Incorrect. The notochord traces back to epiblast cells migrating through the primitive pit and node, not to the roof of the yolk sac -- the yolk sac's own roof lies beneath the notochordal plate at one stage, but is not its source.
explanations.B: Correct. The vertebral bodies form around the notochord from the sclerotome, the ventromedial part of each somite, and once they do, most of the notochord itself degenerates. The notochordal tissue trapped within each developing intervertebral disc is the exception -- it persists rather than degenerating, becoming the nucleus pulposus, the gel-like core of the adult disc.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The notochord runs the length of the embryonic axis, cranial to caudal, and specifically lies cranial to (not caudal to) the cloacal membrane, extending as far forward as the oropharyngeal membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The spinal cord forms from the neural tube, an ectodermal derivative -- the notochord's role there is inductive (it induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate), not a direct contribution of notochordal tissue to the cord itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The vertebral bodies form from sclerotome cells of the somites, which migrate to surround the notochord -- the column forms around the notochord rather than from it, and the notochord itself mostly degenerates except for its nucleus-pulposus remnant.

questions.learning_objective: State that the notochord's only persisting remnant is the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc, while the vertebral column forms around it from sclerotome.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.17, row 86 = b, remark 'Notochord forms nucleus puplosus of intervertebral disc'
field_notes.asu: Embryo 3 Q86, same fact re-tested at Q38 (held as duplicate).

questions.title: Fetal membranes EXCEPT
questions.question: All the following are fetal membranes EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect as an answer -- the umbilical cord is one of the extraembryonic structures conventionally grouped as fetal membranes/appendages.
explanations.B: Incorrect as an answer -- the amnion, the fluid-filled sac surrounding the fetus, is a fetal membrane.
explanations.C: Incorrect as an answer -- the placenta, the site of maternal-fetal exchange, is a fetal (extraembryonic) structure grouped with the membranes even though it also has a maternal contribution.
explanations.D: Incorrect as an answer -- the yolk sac, though it shrinks and becomes functionally vestigial by term, is one of the fetal membranes.
explanations.E: Correct. The notochord is an intraembryonic axial structure -- part of the embryo proper, not an extraembryonic covering or appendage -- so it is not classed among the fetal membranes at all. It is the one item on this list that belongs to a completely different category (embryonic axial skeleton precursor) rather than to the extraembryonic-structures group the other four options share.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the notochord as an intraembryonic structure, distinct from the extraembryonic fetal membranes.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.19, row 90 = e, remark 'Notochord is not a fetal membrane'

questions.title: What is NOT found in the umbilical cord at full term
questions.question: Which of the following is not found in the normal umbilical cord at full term?

explanations.A: Incorrect as an answer -- the definitive cord retains both umbilical arteries, so a right umbilical artery is normally present.
explanations.B: Incorrect as an answer -- Wharton's jelly, the mucoid connective tissue that packs and protects the cord's vessels, is a normal component of the definitive cord.
explanations.C: Incorrect as an answer -- the left umbilical vein is the one vein that persists to term; the definitive cord is normally found to contain it.
explanations.D: Incorrect as an answer -- a remnant of the allantois persists within the connecting-stalk-derived core of the definitive cord, so some allantoic remnant is normally present, even though its lumen degenerates functionally.
explanations.E: Correct. Early in development the primitive cord carries two umbilical veins, but as the cord matures the right umbilical vein degenerates and obliterates, leaving only the left umbilical vein to carry oxygenated blood back to the fetus at full term. So the right umbilical vein -- unlike the right umbilical artery, which persists -- is the one vessel that is normally absent from the umbilical cord at full term, and that is exactly what this question is testing.

questions.learning_objective: State that the right umbilical vein degenerates, leaving only the left umbilical vein in the definitive cord.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.17, row 11 = e, remark 'Left umbilical vein [is the one that persists]'
field_notes.asu: Embryo 3 Q11, same 2-arteries-1-vein fact re-tested at Q36, Q52 (held as duplicates).

questions.author_notes: Sparse overlay onto CON-DEV-134C8B5E98D759, whose own definition already states the right umbilical vein obliterates, leaving one umbilical vein and two umbilical arteries in the definitive cord.

questions.title: Location of the allantois
questions.question: The allantois is present in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The septum transversum is a separate mass of mesoderm contributing to the diaphragm and the fibrous tissue of the liver -- it does not house the allantois.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chorionic villi are the placental exchange structures growing from the chorion into the intervillous space -- the allantois runs through the connecting stalk toward the chorion, but is not itself located within the villi.
explanations.C: Correct. The allantois is an outpouching of the hindgut that extends into the connecting stalk -- the structure that anchors the embryo to the chorion and later becomes part of the umbilical cord as the disc folds. As the primitive umbilical ring forms, the allantois, together with the umbilical vessels, passes through it within the connecting stalk, and its remnant persists there as part of the definitive cord's core.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The amniotic cavity is the fluid-filled space that comes to surround the embryo as folding proceeds -- the allantois is a solid-walled outpouching within the connecting stalk, not a location inside the amniotic cavity itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The placenta is the site of maternal-fetal exchange, formed from chorionic villi and decidua -- the allantois is a cord structure, not a placental one, though its vessels do extend toward the placenta as the umbilical vessels.

questions.learning_objective: State that the allantois lies within the connecting stalk.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.17, row 22 = c, remark 'Allantois lies within connecting stalk'

questions.author_notes: Sparse overlay onto CON-DEV-134C8B5E98D759, whose own definition already states the allantois passes through the primitive umbilical ring within the connecting stalk.

questions.title: Contents of the primitive umbilical cord EXCEPT
questions.question: The primitive umbilical cord contains all the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect as an answer -- the vitelline duct, connecting the secondary yolk sac to the midgut, is a normal content of the primitive cord.
explanations.B: Incorrect as an answer -- one umbilical vein (with the right one already obliterating) is present in the primitive cord, matching the definitive cord's later single-vein state.
explanations.C: Incorrect as an answer -- the allantois, with its remnant of the connecting stalk, is a normal content of the primitive cord.
explanations.D: Correct. Unlike the umbilical vein, where reduction to one vessel happens early, the primitive cord still contains two umbilical arteries, not one -- both umbilical arteries persist all the way to the definitive cord. So 'one umbilical artery' is the false statement here: the true count, at this stage and at full term alike, is two.
explanations.E: Incorrect as an answer -- a portion of the extraembryonic coelom is normally found within the primitive cord (it is only later obliterated as the amnion expands to sheath the cord's contents).

questions.learning_objective: State that both umbilical arteries are present from the primitive cord stage onward, unlike the umbilical vein, which reduces to one.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.19, row 94 = d, remark 'Primitive umbilical cord contains 2 umbilical arteries'

questions.author_notes: Sparse overlay onto CON-DEV-134C8B5E98D759, whose own definition already states the definitive (and, by the same vessel history, primitive) cord holds two umbilical arteries.

questions.title: Umbilical cord anomalies EXCEPT
questions.question: As regards anomalies of the umbilical cord, the following are true EXCEPT:

options.A: A long cord may coil around the neck of the fetus
options.B: A short cord may cause early placental separation
options.C: A true knot is due to local accumulation of Wharton's jelly
options.D: A false knot does not affect the fetus
options.E: In battledore placenta, the cord is attached to the margin of the placenta

explanations.A: Incorrect as an answer -- an excessively long cord can indeed coil around the fetal neck (nuchal cord), a genuine anomaly of length.
explanations.B: Incorrect as an answer -- a short cord can restrict fetal movement and, during delivery, can pull and separate the placenta prematurely, a genuine anomaly of length.
explanations.C: Correct. Local accumulation of Wharton's jelly, or a wider curve of an umbilical vessel, produces a FALSE knot -- a benign, harmless swelling that only looks like a knot -- not a TRUE knot, which is an actual loop of the cord pulled tight, from excessive fetal movement in a long cord. This statement reverses that pairing, attributing Wharton's-jelly accumulation to the true knot instead of the false one, which is why it is the false statement here.
explanations.D: Incorrect as an answer -- a false knot (unlike a tightened true knot, which can compress the vessels and compromise the fetus) causes the fetus no stress, so this statement is true.
explanations.E: Incorrect as an answer -- battledore placenta, marginal cord attachment, is a genuine and correctly described anomaly of attachment (the same fact tested directly at embryo3-q004).

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish a true knot (a real loop, from a long cord and fetal movement) from a false knot (Wharton's-jelly or vessel-curve heaping, harmless).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.19, row 95 = c, remark 'Accumulation of Wharton jelly causes false knots'

questions.author_notes: Sparse overlay onto CON-DEV-3E918A4C74B56D, whose own pitfall note already states this exact false-knot/Wharton's-jelly mechanism.

questions.title: The definitive yolk sac
questions.question: The definitive yolk sac:

options.B: Has a wall made of ectoderm
options.C: Is found in the umbilical cord
options.D: May be found in the amniotic cavity

explanations.A: Incorrect. The yolk sac's cavity is lined by endoderm at every stage (primary, secondary and definitive), not mesoderm -- mesoderm covers its outer surface (the splanchnopleuric layer) rather than lining its lumen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The yolk sac wall is endodermal in its lining, with an outer mesodermal covering -- not ectodermal at any stage.
explanations.C: Correct. As the secondary yolk sac shrinks with folding, its remaining connection to the midgut narrows down to the vitelline duct. What is left outside the abdomen, distal to that narrowing, becomes the definitive yolk sac -- a small vestigial remnant. It persists as part of the umbilical cord's contents, still identifiable near the cord within the membranes at term.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The definitive yolk sac is a remnant located within the umbilical cord/chorionic membranes, not free within the amniotic cavity itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The yolk sac derives from the hypoblast/endoderm lineage (via Heuser's membrane lining the blastocoele, then the secondary yolk sac forming from endoderm), not from the trophoblast, which instead gives rise to the placenta's own epithelial components.

questions.learning_objective: State that the definitive yolk sac is the remnant persisting within the umbilical cord.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.19, row 91 = c, remark 'Definitive yolk sac lies within the umbilical cord'

questions.title: The allantois's own origin
questions.question: As regards the allantois, choose the correct statement:

options.A: Is a diverticulum of the hindgut
options.C: Is an outpouching of the coelom into the connecting stalk
options.D: Is not found in the umbilical cord at any time

explanations.A: Correct. The allantois begins as a diverticulum, an outpouching, of the hindgut. It buds from the endoderm of the caudal part of the yolk sac/hindgut region into the connecting stalk. This gives it an endodermal origin, distinct from the umbilical vessels and the Wharton's jelly it simply runs alongside within the cord.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The allantois does not completely degenerate -- its lumen becomes non-functional and most of it regresses (contributing fibrously to the urachus/median umbilical ligament postnatally), but a remnant persists rather than vanishing entirely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The allantois is a diverticulum of the hindgut (endoderm), not an outpouching of the coelom -- the extraembryonic coelom is a separate, mesoderm-lined cavity that happens to run through the same connecting stalk alongside the allantois, but the allantois itself is not made of coelomic outpouching.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The allantois, or its remnant, is found in the umbilical cord from the primitive-cord stage onward (tested directly at embryo3-q022 and embryo3-q094) -- it is not absent from the cord at every stage.
explanations.E: Incorrect as an answer -- since B, C and D are each false, 'all the above' cannot be the correct choice; only A is correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that the allantois is a hindgut (endodermal) diverticulum, and reject the coelom-outpouching and complete-degeneration distractors.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.19, row 99 = a, remark 'Allantois is a diverticulum of the hindgut'
field_notes.asu: Embryo 3 Q99, complements Q22 (allantois location) and Q94 (allantois present in the primitive cord) rather than duplicating either.

questions.title: Functions of amnion EXCEPT
questions.question: As regards amnion, all the following are true EXCEPT:

options.B: It acts as a protective water jacket for the body
options.D: It is a medium for excretion of urine
options.E: It forms the bag of forewaters during labor

explanations.A: Incorrect as an answer -- amniotic fluid is indeed a clear watery fluid, so this statement is true.
explanations.B: Incorrect as an answer -- in early pregnancy especially, amniotic fluid genuinely acts as a shock-absorbing, protective water jacket around the embryo/fetus, so this statement is true.
explanations.C: Correct. In late pregnancy amniotic fluid does the opposite of preventing fetal movement -- it provides the space the fetus needs to move freely, and those movements are what help develop fetal muscle tone and strength. So 'it prevents fetal movements' reverses the real relationship and is the false statement here.
explanations.D: Incorrect as an answer -- amniotic fluid is genuinely a medium into which fetal urine is excreted from mid-pregnancy onward, so this statement is true.
explanations.E: Incorrect as an answer -- the fore bag of amniotic fluid, ahead of the presenting part, genuinely helps the cervix dilate gradually during labour and is called the bag of forewaters, so this statement is true.

questions.learning_objective: State that amniotic fluid provides space that helps, rather than prevents, fetal movement.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.19, row 93 = c, remark 'Amnion helps fetal movements'

questions.author_notes: Sparse overlay onto CON-DEV-F356C3B8CFD31E, whose own definition already states amniotic fluid 'provides space for the fetal movements that develop the fetal muscles' in late pregnancy.
